articles.title: 'Mr C Joseph hates Sanatan': BJP hits out at Vijay govt after SC's Deepam rebuke
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The BJP on Friday slammed the Tamil Nadu government after the Supreme Court issued contempt notices to senior state officials over the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The BJP on Friday slammed the Tamil Nadu government after the Supreme Court issued contempt notices to senior state officials over the Karthigai Deepam row, accusing chief minister C Joseph Vijay of deliberately violating constitutional principles and hurting the religious sentiments of Hindu devotees.BJP national president Nitin Nabin also hailed the SC order saying, "A historic victory for every devotee of Lord Murugan! By ordering the ceremonial lamp to be lit at the Thiruparankundram Deepathoon tomorrow and pulling up Tamil Nadu authorities for acting at the dictates of their political bosses, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has thoroughly exposed the INDI Alliance government's anti-Sanatan mindset.""No political conspiracy can stop the sacred traditions of Bharat. May the divine blessings of Lord Murugan protect all devotees and guide them on the path of courage and righteousness," he added.Meanwhile, addressing a press conference, BJP national spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia alleged that the controversy had arisen because of the state government's hostility towards Sanatan traditions and the Hindu community."This press conference is being held on a very important issue relating to the Karthigai Deepam row, which has been created only because the government in Tamil Nadu and the chief minister there, Mr C Joseph, hate Sanatan traditions and the Hindu community. This hatred is so deep that a chief minister who has taken an oath to protect and preserve the ethos of the Constitution has, prima facie, wilfully decided to violate it," Bhatia said.BJP leader CR Kesavan also criticised the state government, calling the Supreme Court's direction to light the ceremonial lamp at the Deepathoon on Saturday a victory for devotees of Lord Muruga."The sacred Karthigai Deepam, which will now be lit at the Deepathoon atop Thiruparankundram Hill tomorrow, is indeed an emphatic victory and a true triumph for the implicit faith and sentiments of crores of Lord Muruga devotees," Kesavan said.He accused the state government of using the controversy for political gains and alleged that its actions had hurt the sentiments of Hindu devotees."The dubious and dangerous divisive drama enacted and orchestrated by the TVK Congress government to perpetrate their vote-bank politics of communal appeasement deeply hurt and humiliated the sentiments of countless Hindu devotees," he said.Kesavan further demanded an unconditional apology from Vijay, saying, "This TVK Congress government, led by Joseph Vijay needs to tender an unconditional apology immediately to the people of Tamil Nadu and crores of Lord Muruga devotees for betraying their faith."The row centres on the lighting of the traditional Karthigai Deepam lamp atop the Deepathoon, a stone pillar on Thiruparankundram hill in Tamil Nadu's Madurai district. The dispute escalated after the Madras High Court directed that the ceremonial lamp be lit at the pillar, amid objections and competing claims over the site.On November 20, the Supreme Court permitted the lighting of the lamp at Deepathoon on November 24 as a one-time interim arrangement. However, the ceremonial flame was lit only at the customary Uchaipillaiyar mandapam and not at the disputed pillar, prompting contempt proceedings.Then earlier Friday, the Supreme Court directed that the traditional lamp be lit atop Deepathoon on Saturday using the flame lit at the Uchaipillaiyar mandapam. It also issued contempt notices to Tamil Nadu Chief Secretary, Director General of Police, Madurai Collector and other officials over the alleged non-compliance with its earlier order.The bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi observed that the state executive authorities appeared to have acted on the "diktats of their political bosses" and said wilful non-compliance with court orders would have to be dealt with an "iron hand".The court also suspended the temple's board of trustees, appointed two retired Madras High Court judges as receivers to take over its management, and handed over security of the temple and Thiruparankundram hill to the CRPF.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A US World War II veteran was wounded in Germany in 1945 but never received his Purple Heart; at 99, he finally received the medal 81 years later
articles.summary: A 99-year-old US World War II veteran who was wounded by enemy shellfire in Germany in March 1945 has finally received his Purple Heart, 81 years after
articles.body: A 99-year-old US World War II veteran who was wounded by enemy shellfire in Germany in March 1945 has finally received his Purple Heart, 81 years after the incident. Glenn Fisher, who served with the 556th Anti-Aircraft Artillery Unit, was injured in an attack that killed two of his comrades, but never received the medal because of problems with his military records. After more than a year of efforts by his longtime friend Jeff Thoke to overcome the documentation hurdles, Fisher was presented with the award at a ceremony at the Frazier Kentucky History Museum on July 1, 2026.Why did a World War II veteran wait 81 years for his Purple HeartAccording to the Frazier Kentucky History Museum, Fisher was injured in March 1945 while serving with the 556th Anti-Aircraft Artillery Unit in Germany. Enemy shells struck and exploded, injuring 14 members of his unit. Two of his comrades were killed in the incident, including his close friend Paul Baker.As per the Museum, Fisher sustained shrapnel injuries to his face and the area near his hip. The museum's earlier account also revealed that some of the shrapnel remained inside his body for nearly 80 years. Additional shrapnel was removed just three years before the 2026 ceremony. While the details of those who died in the attack were well documented, records concerning the injured soldiers were not as complete, creating difficulties when Fisher sought his Purple Heart.How did a friend help Fisher finally secure his ‘Purple Heart’ awardThe delay in receiving the Purple Heart was linked to an incorrectly recorded date of Fisher's injury. Those wounded in the incident initially received treatment at a field hospital. Fisher's longtime friend Jeff Thoke, who is also associated with Bluegrass Honour Flights, took on the task of helping him obtain the award. He spent months working through the paperwork and attempting to overcome the administrative obstacles. However, the US Army initially rejected the requests because of insufficient documentation. Thoke continued his efforts for more than a year to establish the evidence needed to secure the recognition.On March 23, 2026, the Frazier Kentucky History Museum held a news conference to bring attention to Fisher's case. The event aimed to highlight his wartime service and the difficulties he had faced in receiving the medal. At the time, Fisher was approaching his 100th birthday, and the museum's account stressed the urgency of resolving the matter while he was still alive to receive the award.Rachel Platt, VP of Mission at the Frazier Kentucky History Museum, who had previously known Fisher through her work as a journalist covering Honour Flights for veterans travelling to Washington, DC, helped bring his story to wider attention. Fisher had enlisted in the US Army with his parents' permission and was just 16 years old when he joined, following the December 7, 1941, attack on Pearl Harbour.What happened when Fisher finally received his Purple HeartFisher's long wait finally ended on July 1, 2026, when he received his Purple Heart during a ceremony at the Frazier Kentucky History Museum. Major Francisco Bonglo, from the US Army's Awards and Decorations Branch, pinned the medal on the 99-year-old veteran.The ceremony also featured Heather French Henry, Miss America 2000, who sang the national anthem. articles.title: A Canadian couple said a 1997 access agreement let them drive past their lakeside house over a developer's land, but an alleged 46-square-metre encroachment led to a fight; a BC court rejected their claim to that route
articles.summary: A Canadian couple argued that an old access agreement let them drive across a developer's land to reach their lakeside home, but a British Columbia court
articles.body: A Canadian couple argued that an old access agreement let them drive across a developer's land to reach their lakeside home, but a British Columbia court ruled against them on a key part of their case, deciding that the disputed stretch of road was not covered by the agreement. The fight centered on a vacation property next to Upper Arrow Lake in British Columbia, where Jeno and Luminita Fabian said they had the right to use a road that ran across land owned by property developer Halcyon Point Development ULC.On 25 November 2026, the Supreme Court of British Columbia ruled that an easement registered in 1997 did not give the couple the right to use the disputed land north of their house, and it also turned down their backup request for a statutory easement over that land. In her ruling, Justice Lyster found that the agreement covered only the road that existed when the easement was granted, and the evidence did not show that the northern section was part of that road in 1997. The ruling, reported in Halcyon Point Development ULC v. Fabian, 2026 BCSC 2289, settles how to read the access agreement while leaving other claims between the neighbours to be handled later in separate proceedings.How the access agreement became a legal disputeHalcyon owns a 16.31-acre property called District Lot 2683 on the east side of Upper Arrow Lake, while the Fabians own a neighbouring vacation property, Lot 4, of about 0.52 acres, where their lakeside house sits. According to the court judgment, drivers can reach the couple's property only by using a road across Halcyon's land and another neighbouring property, Lot 3. An easement registered in 1997 gave owners of several lots, including Lot 4, the right to cross the developer's land, letting people, vehicles, animals and equipment use the existing road.The argument began over what counted as the road when the agreement was registered. The Fabians said the route included a northern branch running past the north side of their house toward the lake, whereas Halcyon said the original road covered only a southern section and that a northern extension was built later. This difference mattered because part of today's driveway reaches past the Fabians' property line onto Halcyon's land.Disputed section measured about 71 square metresThe land at the center of the fight was about 17 metres long and 4.2 metres wide, covering roughly 71 square metres. The Fabians said they needed the extra space so larger vehicles could reach the front door of their home and service the septic tank. The judgment notes that the shortest gap between the north corner of the house and the property line was about 3.4 metres, and the couple said that space was too tight for larger vehicles, so they needed to use the neighbouring land. They said septic trucks needed to drive through the area once or twice a year to empty the tank, and delivery trucks bringing appliances or furniture also needed access to the front of the house from time to time. Halcyon disagreed that the couple needed to cross its land, arguing that the 3.4-metre space was wide enough for vehicles to reach the home without crossing onto its property. The fight was not just about the route, as the neighbours also argued over where their shared property line sat.Survey exposed the extent of the encroachmentWhere the boundary sat became another point of conflict after the Fabians bought their property in August 2011. The couple said survey markers were already there when they bought the land, and they thought those markers showed the true northern boundary. In July 2023, Halcyon's principal, Dale Tortorelli, accused Jeno Fabian of moving the markers farther north to make his backyard bigger, which Fabian denied. The couple also said Tortorelli assaulted Fabian during a clash on 5 August 2023 and then moved the markers despite objections, a version Tortorelli disputed while saying the two men had several heated arguments and that he called the Royal Canadian Mounted Police once. The court did not rule on those claims as part of the easement application.Both sides hired land surveyors in August and October 2023, and both surveys reached the same result, showing that the original markers were in the wrong spot before surveyors put them on the right line to settle that issue. A later survey ordered by the Fabians in April 2026 put the disputed overlap at 46.2 square metres. According to the survey by Tracey Peet of Selkirk Land Surveying, the road was three metres wide on the couple's side of the line and 4.5 metres wide on Halcyon's land, and a ditch about one metre deep also ran between the house and the edge of the road.Court examined photographs and earlier property recordsJustice Lyster looked at whether the northern part of the driveway was there when the easement was registered in 1997. The Fabians pointed to property appraisal photos from August 2010 and June 2011, arguing they showed the northern route and backed their claim that it was part of the original road. However, the judge found that the photos showed bare ground north of the house rather than a built road, and did not show that the bare ground stretched across the property line onto District Lot 2683. The court also reviewed aerial photos showing that vehicles could use the area as it looks today, yet those photos did not show what the route looked like when the agreement was signed.Halcyon pointed to evidence from Tortorelli, who said there was no road north of the house before the Fabians bought the property in 2011. He also said the couple built a carport south of their house that blocked access from the existing driveway, and added that they brought in large amounts of fill in May 2024 to build a terrace between the house and the lake, while maintaining that vehicles could still reach the front of the house without crossing onto its land. After looking at the evidence, Justice Lyster decided that the original road looped back toward Lot 3 south of the house and did not have a northern branch crossing the boundary, adding that the Fabians had the duty to prove that the disputed area was part of the original easement and did not prove it.Alternative request for a new easement rejectedAfter their argument over the 1997 deal failed, the Fabians asked the court to grant a new statutory easement under section 36(2) of British Columbia's Property Law Act. That law lets the Supreme Court grant an easement, transfer ownership, or order the removal of an encroachment in certain cases involving a building crossing onto a neighbour's land or a fence wrongly enclosing another property. The couple argued that the law should be read broadly enough to cover their disputed driveway, pointing to earlier court rulings that read "building" or "fence" more broadly in encroachment cases, including cases about access roads.Halcyon opposed the request, arguing that a plain dirt road is neither a building nor a fence under the law, and Justice Lyster agreed with the developer. The judge reviewed earlier rulings, including Bland v. Bland and Allen v. 0990199, to see if the disputed area fit the definitions in the law, and found in the judgment that the overlap was not a fence, never held one, and was not a building, a structure with walls and a roof, or a key part of the couple's house. The judge said larger vehicles used the disputed area now and then to reach the front of the property, but that use was not enough to bring it under section 36(2), so the court ruled it had no power to grant the statutory easement the Fabians wanted and did not need to decide if extra access would be fair or convenient because the legal test for using that power was not met.Remaining allegations still to be resolvedThe ruling focused on how to read the existing easement and on the couple's backup request for a statutory right of access, leaving the broader legal fight between the neighbours separate. Halcyon originally filed a civil claim saying the Fabians trespassed on its land by building a road and parking area and adding other features, including gardens and recreation spots, while asking for an injunction and damages for trespass and nuisance. The Fabians denied trespassing and filed a counterclaim against Halcyon and Tortorelli, saying Tortorelli trespassed on their property and assaulted Jeno Fabian and asking for damages and other remedies, claims that were not decided in this application and remain part of the wider case.In her 25 November judgment, Justice Lyster granted the request to separate the property questions from the rest of the claims, dismissed the Fabians' request to treat the northern road as part of the 1997 easement, and rejected their backup request under the Property Law Act. Halcyon was found to have succeeded in large part on the issues decided and was awarded its costs for the application, in any event of the cause.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Not only Rubio, Hegseth and Bessent: Around half a dozen Trump officials move into military housing amid 'security threats'
articles.summary: Around half a dozen members of US President Donald Trump's administration are now living in military accommodation in Washington DC, traditionally
articles.body: Around half a dozen members of US President Donald Trump's administration are now living in military accommodation in Washington DC, traditionally reserved for senior military officers and top defence officials, amid rising domestic political violence and what officials describe as emerging threats from foreign adversaries, particularly Iran, CNN reported.Treasury secretary Scott Bessent is the latest known Cabinet member to move into military housing. He recently left his mansion in Georgetown and relocated to a secure military base in Washington.Bessent joins secretary of state Marco Rubio, defence secretary Pete Hegseth, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and several other Trump administration officials who have already moved into military residences. Many of these homes, some more than a century old, are located within access-controlled military compounds and offer enhanced security.US attorney general Todd Blanche has also recently moved to a military base over security concerns, according to people familiar with the matter. His predecessor, Pam Bondi, had similarly lived at a military installation last year.Meanwhile, Miller, his wife Katie and their four children moved from their Virginia home into military accommodation last year after protests were held outside their residence and flyers carrying their home address were circulated.Military housing comes at a costCabinet officials residing in military housing are required to pay rent, which typically exceeds USD 4,500 per month, depending on the property.The current rental arrangement dates back to former defence secretary Robert Gates, who served under Presidents George W Bush and Barack Obama and became the first Pentagon chief to live in military accommodation.Former secretary of state Mike Pompeo, who served under Trump, also sought military housing in 2018. However, the Navy initially described his request as "problematic" due to "factual, legal, fiscal, and ethical issues", according to an internal Navy memo.The memo flagged concerns over the "appearance of impropriety… relating to a civilian secretary of state displacing a uniformed member of the military in a tight housing market". It also pointed to a waiting list for housing among Navy flag officers at the time.Pompeo eventually took up residence in military accommodation at Fort Myer in Virginia.Move raises scrutinyThe growing presence of civilian political appointees in military housing has drawn criticism from Democratic lawmakers, who have expressed concerns over the use of facilities intended for military personnel and the rental arrangements involved.Representative George Whitesides of California secured the House Armed Services Committee's approval for a report examining the issue. The Pentagon has been directed to submit the report by spring, detailing the political appointees living in military accommodation, the security threats prompting their relocation, the legal basis for the arrangements and the rent they pay.Whitesides maintained that the inquiry was necessary to ensure accountability in the use of military residences by civilian officials. He stressed the need to examine "politically-appointed officials living in housing designated for military members to ensure they are paying fair market rates."The issue has also come under the spotlight following questions over spending on military residences. Defence secretary Pete Hegseth faced criticism last year after lawmakers discovered that the Army was preparing to spend USD 137,297 on repairs and upgrades to his residence at Fort McNair.(With ANI inputs)You use AI every day. articles.title: South Australian police withdraw 8,383 speeding fines worth $4.7 million after a technical compliance issue; more than 70,000 motorists who already paid will not receive refunds
articles.summary: South Australian police withdraw over 8,000 speeding fines amounting to $4.7 million after a compliance issue with mobile speed camera testing. However, more than 70,000 paid fines will not be refunded.
articles.body: South Australian police are withdrawing 8,383 speeding fines worth approximately $4.7 million after identifying a technical compliance issue involving mobile speed cameras. However, more than 70,000 motorists who have already paid their penalties will not receive refunds, ABC News reported.The decision, announced by Acting Assistant Commissioner Scott Fitzgerald, also covers 13 cases that are already before the courts. The affected notices were issued between November 6, 2025, and October 29.The issue relates to the procedures followed when mobile speed cameras were tested at the beginning of their daily operations. Police said the problem concerned compliance with Australian Standards governing part of the testing process, rather than the accuracy of the cameras themselves.Why are South Australian police withdrawing the speeding fines?According to Fitzgerald, a non-compliance concern was raised during court proceedings last month. An internal review subsequently identified a technical issue involving the timing of routine tests required before mobile speed cameras begin operating.He said the tests had been carried out during operations rather than beforehand, as required under the relevant Australian Standard."This is a technical evidentiary issue and not an accuracy issue," Fitzgerald said, adding that the problem did not mean the cameras had malfunctioned or failed to detect motorists exceeding speed limits.SA Police said it had complied with the requirements of the Road Traffic Regulations but had not met the Australian Standard. The department attributed the situation to differences in the wording of the two sets of requirements.Fitzgerald said police changed their procedures after identifying the problem. The revised mobile speed camera deployment process came into effect on October 29, 2026.The withdrawal applies only to fines issued through mobile speed cameras. Penalties recorded by fixed speed cameras, hand-held devices, point-to-point systems or police officers are not covered by the decision.Why will motorists who have paid their fines not get refunds?Although 8,383 outstanding fines are being withdrawn, the decision will not extend to motorists who have already settled their penalties.SA Police said 70,184 fines issued by mobile speed cameras during the affected period had been paid. Those motorists will not receive their money back.Fitzgerald maintained that the cameras were accurate and that the compliance issue did not establish that motorists had been wrongly identified as speeding. He acknowledged that the decision could cause frustration among those affected.The distinction lies in the evidentiary requirements governing the camera testing process, rather than an identified problem with the devices' ability to measure vehicle speeds.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1977, Soviet test pilot Aleksandr Fedotov took a MiG-25 to 37,650 metres, more than 23 miles above Earth; the powered-aircraft altitude record is still listed as current
articles.summary: Discover the incredible feat of Soviet test pilot Aleksandr Fedotov as he sets the unbeatable MiG-25 altitude record of 37,650 metres in 1977, a milestone that remains unbroken in aviation history.
articles.body: Soviet test pilot Aleksandr Vasilyevich Fedotov climbed 37,650 metres above Podmoskovnoye, near Moscow, on August 31, 1977. He set a record in aviation altitude, and his flight to this day remains on the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale’s (FAI) current list of world records. A modified version of the MiG-25, designated E-266M, was used for this experiment. The aircraft pushed the limits of what a self-powered aeroplane could achieve while reaching an altitude of more than 23 miles above Earth during its flight. The record is listed under the FAI’s C-Absolute category for Powered Aeroplanes as ratified and current.Fedotov graduated from the Moscow Aviation Institute in 1958. The same year he began working with the Mikoyan design bureau. Throughout his career as a pilot, he had tested other aircraft from the MiG lot such as the MiG-19, MiG-21, MiG-23, MiG-25, MiG-29 and MiG-31. After being named the Hero of the Soviet Union in 1966 and he also attained the rank of Major-General of Aviation in later years. The 1977 flight by the pilot remains an important record in his career because it established an altitude mark in a specific category of powered aviation that is yet to be surpassed.The aircraft used for the experiment behind the recordThe MiG-25, which is known by the NATO reporting name Foxbat, was developed by the Soviet Union. The intention behind developing it was to make a high-speed interceptor and reconnaissance aircraft. Two powerful turbojet engines and a substantial airframe were used for the aircraft. Moreover, the majority of it was constructed from nickel steel to withstand the aerodynamic heating that is associated with extreme-speed flight. These characteristics are crucial in making the MiG-25 a platform for testing the limits of high-altitude performance, though the record-setting E-266M was a modified experimental aircraft instead of an ordinary operational interceptor.As per Air & Space Forces Magazine, the E-266M was already part of a bigger programme of experimental flights which reportedly used the MiG-25 design to establish the speed and climbing records. As earlier experiments showed some promising results, the programme continued with modifications with the intention of improving its capabilities. Reportedly, the E-266M was an experimental development with uprated engines.Fedotov had previously established an absolute altitude record on July 25, 1973, when he reached 36,240 metres. Four years later, he continued the record-setting programme, and on July 22, 1977, he reached 37,080 metres with both 1,000-kilogram and 2,000-kilogram payloads, according to the FAI world-record database. The flight in August that followed this was without a payload, and in that he reached 37,650 metres.How the MiG-25 reached more than 37 kilometresFedotov’s record was achieved through a steep climbing manoeuvre instead of maintaining a level flight at that altitude.Guinness World Records has identified the flight as an almost vertical climb. Commonly known as a zoom climb, this kind of flight happens when an aircraft builds up speed at a lower altitude and then pitches upwards while converting some of its forward kinetic energy into height. As the aircraft climbs, its speed falls in thin air. This should not be confused with a sustained horizontal flight, in which an aircraft needs to continue generating enough lift and thrust to maintain a relatively constant altitude. This is the reason why Fedotov’s achievement should not be confused with just any aviation category. The FAI now identifies the 37,650-metre record as the current C-Absolute altitude record for Powered Aeroplanes.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'He can't be a friend': Zelenskyy draws Hitler parallel over Trump's praise for Putin
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has criticised US President Donald Trump's approach towards Russian President Vladimir Putin, saying the Russian
articles.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has criticised US President Donald Trump's approach towards Russian President Vladimir Putin, saying the Russian leader cannot be considered a friend given his role in the invasion of Ukraine."He can’t be a friend," Zelenskyy told the BBC in an interview broadcast on Friday, questioning Trump's description of Putin as "my friend" during a recent summit in China. He said Putin was "an aggressor and a killer" and likened the remark to someone calling Adolf Hitler a friend during World War II.Zelenskyy's remarks come amid growing differences between Kyiv and Washington over how to end the nearly five-year-old war, with the Ukrainian leader urging Trump to put greater pressure on Moscow to halt its invasion.The comments also come as uncertainty grows over continued financial assistance from Europe. European Union leaders failed to reach an agreement on Thursday over a proposed $49 billion loan to meet Ukraine's economic and military requirements next year.Zelenskyy questions US approach towards PutinThe Ukrainian president's criticism followed recent remarks by Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, who is involved in efforts to mediate an end to the conflict, praising Putin as a "grandmaster" of politics.Kushner's partner in the peace efforts, US envoy Steve Witkoff, had also described the Russian president as a "humanitarian" weeks earlier.Zelenskyy's comments drew a sharp response from the Kremlin. Russian presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov accused the Ukrainian leader of "insulting his counterpart", adding that Zelenskyy "is not willing to follow the path of (a) peace settlement."The International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant for Putin over alleged war crimes, holding him personally responsible for the unlawful deportation and transfer of children from Ukraine. The Trump administration has imposed sweeping sanctions on the court as part of its campaign against the tribunal over investigations involving the US and its allies, including Israel.Zelenskyy has also expressed frustration over delays in the delivery of Patriot missile systems that Ukraine has already paid for. The systems are crucial for intercepting Russian ballistic missiles. He has further raised concerns about problems with Starlink's military-grade satellite internet service, which plays a key role in Ukraine's drone operations and military communications.European support for Ukraine faces uncertaintyUkraine's concerns over continued Western assistance have grown after EU leaders failed to agree on a proposed $49 billion loan for the country's economic and military needs next year.Although European governments have repeatedly pledged to support Kyiv against Russia's invasion, political changes across the continent could complicate future commitments. Elections in EU member states over the next 12 months could strengthen parties opposed to providing further financial assistance to Ukraine.Russia's invasion has killed hundreds of thousands of military personnel and thousands of Ukrainian civilians. The conflict has also triggered extensive sanctions against Moscow and left Putin diplomatically isolated in much of the West before Trump renewed engagement with the Russian leader.Nine more Ukrainian children return home from RussiaIn a separate development, nine Ukrainian children were brought back from Russia and Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine on Friday as part of an operation mediated by US First Lady Melania Trump.An eight-year-old boy was among those reunited with their families after nearly five years apart. His mother, Alina Sydorenko, welcomed him at Ukraine's northern border."I want to show him everything that he missed and was taken away from him," she said.Some of the children had lost their parents, who died in occupied territory, and were received by other relatives.Zelenskyy announced the latest operation under the Bring Kids Back UA initiative on social media, thanking Melania Trump for helping mediate the reunifications. The White House said on Wednesday that 43 children had been brought home through her involvement.According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine has so far managed to bring back 2,875 children."We remember each and every one of them. We are doing everything we can to find them and return them to their families," he said.Kyiv seeks to ease concerns over strike in LibyaMeanwhile, Ukraine has sought to reassure Libya and its Western partners after a Ukrainian strike on a Russian naval vessel docked at a Libyan port raised concerns that the conflict could spread beyond Ukraine.Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said he spoke to his Libyan counterpart Al-Taher Al-Baour by phone and conveyed that Kyiv had no intention of drawing Libya into the war.In a statement posted on X late Thursday, Sybiha also reaffirmed Ukraine's support for Libya's sovereignty and efforts to reunify the country.Russian and Ukrainian drone attacks intensifyThe aerial conflict between the two countries has also intensified, with attacks increasingly targeting civilian and critical infrastructure.Russia carried out nearly 300 aerial attacks a week against civilian infrastructure in Ukraine through November 20, according to the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), which tracks political violence and conflict.Zelenskyy warned on Thursday that a major Russian attack was imminent.Ukraine's air force said its air defences intercepted 110 of the 155 Russian drones launched overnight on Friday, including 51 jet-powered Shahed-type drones. However, strikes were reported at 27 locations across the country.The attacks hit railway infrastructure, energy facilities, businesses and residential buildings across nine Ukrainian regions, killing at least one person and injuring at least six, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said.Russia's Defence Ministry, meanwhile, claimed that its forces intercepted 318 Ukrainian drones overnight across 10 Russian regions and Crimea, which Moscow illegally annexed.Residents of St Petersburg reported explosions in eight districts, according to Russian online news outlet Astra. In another attack, 70 apartments in a multi-storey building were damaged in the Black Sea port city of Novorossiysk in Russia's Krasnodar region.Russian officials said the Ukrainian attacks killed at least two people and wounded six others.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Minnesota man bought lakefront land in 2021 and found his neighbour's cabin, outhouse and septic system encroaching on it; in 2026, appeals judges reopened part of the boundary fight and reversed a tree-damage ruling
articles.summary: A Minnesota man who purchased lakefront property in 2021 discovered that his neighbour's cabin, outhouse and septic system extended onto his land.
articles.body: A Minnesota man who purchased lakefront property in 2021 discovered that his neighbour's cabin, outhouse and septic system extended onto his land. The dispute eventually reached court, where the neighbour's family trust claimed ownership of part of the property through long-term use and sought damages over trees removed during the expansion of an access path along a utility easement. However, on November 23, 2026, the Minnesota Court of Appeals reversed part of the lower court's decision, finding that factual disputes remained over a section of land and who had cut down the trees.In its November 23 decision in Gary Ross v. Dennis Hubbard, available on Justia, the Minnesota Court of Appeals affirmed part of the judgment but reversed the rulings on adverse possession of a portion of the disputed land and tree-damage liability, sending those issues back to the lower court.Neighbour's structures extended onto newly purchased landAccording to the court's decision, Gary Ross and the Williams Revocable Family Trust owned adjoining properties along Lake Vermilion in St Louis County. Ross purchased his property in 2021 and commissioned a survey after completing the purchase. The survey revealed that a cabin and subsurface sewage treatment system belonging to the neighbouring property encroached onto his land, identified as Lot 4. An outhouse was also entirely situated on his property.The structures had a long history. The cabin and outhouse were built in the 1950s, before the Williams family purchased the neighbouring property in 1967. In 1979, the family installed the septic system, part of which also extended onto Lot 4. The family had believed that an ash tree located about 25 feet inside Ross's property marked the boundary. They also used portions of the lakeshore to store firewood, canoes and other belongings.After discovering the encroachments, Ross asked the neighbour to remove the satellite dish and stored items. The disagreements eventually led to competing property claims.Trust claimed ownership through long-term useRoss filed a lawsuit seeking to establish trespass and recover possession of the affected land. The Williams family trust responded with counterclaims, including adverse possession, trespass and nuisance. Adverse possession allows someone to acquire legal ownership of land by actually possessing it in an open, hostile, continuous and exclusive manner for the legally required period. In Minnesota, the required period is 15 years.The district court granted summary judgment in favour of the trust, finding that it had established adverse possession over the entire disputed eastern 25-foot portion of Lot 4. The court also ruled that Ross was responsible for removing trees from the neighbouring property and awarded the trust $106,890 in treble damages, which means three times the assessed damages. Ross challenged both findings before the Court of Appeals.Appeals court reopens part of boundary disputeThe appeals judges agreed that the trust had established adverse possession over the front portion of Lot 4, extending from the lakeshore to the northernmost point of an existing trail. However, they found that the evidence did not establish the same claim for the back portion, which extended from the trail towards the public road.The court noted that the family's predecessors had constructed buildings, while the family had installed equipment and stored personal belongings on the front portion. These activities provided evidence of ownership over the required period. But the back portion had largely remained in its natural, wooded state. There was insufficient evidence of visible acts demonstrating that the family had openly occupied that section as its own.The judges therefore found that a genuine factual dispute remained over whether the previous owners had received clear notice that the neighbouring family was claiming ownership of the back portion. The court reversed the summary judgment on that part of the adverse-possession claim and sent it back for further proceedings. The trust's claim to the front portion remained undisturbed.Court reverses $106,890 tree-damage awardThe appeals court also examined the dispute over trees removed to create an expanded access path along a utility easement. Ross maintained that the local electric utility had removed the trees while installing a powerline in November 2021. However, the trust's representative disputed this, stating that a utility employee had told him the company had not constructed the path. Neither side provided direct evidence from the utility establishing who had carried out the work.The judges found that the competing accounts created a genuine issue of material fact. Since the identity of the person responsible for cutting the trees was unresolved, the lower court could not establish Ross's liability through summary judgment. Consequently, the appeals court reversed the summary judgment on the trespass-to-chattels claim and the $106,890 treble-damages award, remanding the issue for further proceedings.Case sent back for further proceedingsOn November 23, 2026, the Minnesota Court of Appeals affirmed the lower court's decision in part, reversed it in part and remanded the case.The ruling preserves the trust's ownership claim over the front portion of the disputed land but reopens the question of ownership over the back portion. It also removes the existing tree-damage award pending further examination of who actually removed the trees. The decision is nonprecedential under Minnesota's appellate rules.You use AI every day. articles.title: UK's Department for Work and Pensions takes nearly all its online services offline after a cyber incident, hitting Universal Credit, PIP and pension applications while benefit payments continue
articles.summary: People across the UK trying to claim Universal Credit, apply for disability support or check their state pension were unable to use most online services
articles.body: People across the UK trying to claim Universal Credit, apply for disability support or check their state pension were unable to use most online services on Friday, 27 November 2026, after the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) took its systems offline following a cyber incident. Officials said regular benefit and pension payments were still being made as normal while work continued to restore the services. The shutdown began as a safety measure after unusual activity was detected on Thursday night, according to The Guardian and Insurance Business. Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden described it as a "serious cyber incident". He said there was no evidence so far that personal data had been exposed, but added that the investigation was still under way.Services hit while payouts keep flowingOnline services for Universal Credit sign-ins and applications, Personal Independence Payment (PIP) applications and pension services were taken offline on Friday morning, according to Identity Week and Computer Weekly. The government's job-search service was also unavailable. Some users reported problems signing in to their Universal Credit accounts and reporting income from self-employment, The Guardian and Computer Weekly reported. Reports of problems accessing DWP services began late on Thursday night and reached their highest level shortly before 9.00am on Friday, according to monitoring website Downdetector, as cited by Computer Weekly. The bereavement service known as "Tell Us Once" was also affected, Identity Week reported. Despite the loss of online services, the DWP said on GOV.UK that regular benefit and pension payments would continue as normal. People who need help have been advised to call their usual benefit helpline. The relevant phone numbers are listed on GOV.UK. Those trying to use the affected online services have also been advised to try again later.Debbie Abrahams, Labour chair of the work and pensions committee, supported the decision to take the services offline. In comments reported by The Guardian, she said: "The DWP has taken swift action to contain any potential further damage from the cyber incident and so that service is restored as soon as possible. Although this may interrupt some services, this was absolutely the right thing to do. It's critical that the impact on service users from the outage is investigated and analysed so that timely and accurate advice can be given to them."Ministers and cyber teams investigate the causeThe DWP is working with GCHQ's National Cyber Security Centre and the Government Cyber Coordination Centre to find out what happened and restore its online services, according to the department's notice on GOV.UK. Officials have not yet confirmed what caused the disruption or who may have been responsible. A Downing Street spokesperson told reporters that the investigation was continuing and would not rule out the possibility of a hack. However, the spokesperson said there was no evidence that a malicious actor was targeting other government departments, according to The Guardian and ITV News. Cybernews reported that officials had said the incident was not ransomware and did not involve money being moved. McFadden said the department received reports of a cyber incident on Thursday and took its systems offline to protect the public and their personal information. He said regular payments had continued throughout the disruption.Speaking to the media, McFadden said:"We had reports of a cyber incident yesterday, and as a precautionary measure, we've taken our systems down in order to protect the public. There's no evidence of anyone's personal details being compromised, although it is an ongoing investigation, and regular payments to the public are continuing as normal. It's a serious cyber incident, I can't say more at this stage about what caused the incident, but we did the right thing by taking our systems down in order to protect the public, in order to protect their personal information, and made sure that regular payments could continue unaffected. We are working with the national cyber security centre to try to get our systems back up and running as quickly as possible, and that effort is ongoing and it's the whole focus of the department right now."Warnings over scams and wider security risksCybersecurity experts have warned people claiming benefits to be alert to scams that could take advantage of the disruption. Luis Costa, from cybersecurity firm Surfshark, told The Guardian that fraudsters might pretend to be DWP staff and offer help with accounts. They could also claim that benefit payments are at risk unless people quickly confirm their personal details. Costa advised people not to share bank details, personal information or security codes. He also warned them not to click on suspicious links or pay unexpected fees. People who receive unexpected calls should hang up and contact the DWP using the official details on GOV.UK instead. The department also reminded the public on GOV.UK that it will never ask for personal information by text message or email.The outage comes just days after a government alert warned that the risk of Russian sabotage attacks in the UK had increased, particularly against businesses that support Ukraine. It also follows a suspected cyberattack earlier in November that affected supermarket refrigeration systems in seven European countries, The Guardian and Insurance Business reported. Earlier this month, DWP permanent secretary Sarah Healey told MPs on the work and pensions select committee that cybersecurity and the ability to keep services running during disruptions were among the issues that concerned her most, The Guardian reported. The DWP is continuing to work with national cyber agencies to restore its online services. However, people who need to use the affected portals face an uncertain wait, as the department has not announced when all services are expected to be available again.You use AI every day. articles.title: A New Zealand couple built a four-bedroom home using 1,300 recycled tyres and 7,000 glass bottles; after appearing on Grand Designs, their Earthship is now looking for a new owner
articles.summary: A four-bedroom home made using 1,300 recycled tyres and 7,000 glass bottles has been put up for sale in New Zealand's Coromandel region.
articles.body: A four-bedroom home made using 1,300 recycled tyres and 7,000 glass bottles has been put up for sale in New Zealand's Coromandel region. The property featured in the first season of Grand Designs New Zealand. Its owners, Gus Anning and Sarah Rowe, are selling Earthship Te Timatanga in rural Hikuai as they prepare to move north to the Bay of Islands. The house was built in 2015 and is located at 189 Puketui Valley Road. It uses passive heating, solar power, rainwater collection and greywater systems. According to a OneRoof report by Diana Clement, the property is listed with Bayleys agents Heather Sturgeon and Sandie Faiers. It is the first time the home has been offered for sale.How a film sparked the buildRowe and Anning began dreaming of building an Earthship home in New Zealand after watching the documentary Garbage Warrior, according to OneRoof. They found a site in rural Hikuai that matched their plans. The valley, mountain peak and river nearby made it an ideal place for their project."Literally, it's an absolutely gorgeous valley with a peak staring at you right in the face, with a beautiful river," Anning said, as reported by OneRoof. "It ticked all the boxes for that dream section, really."The couple worked with local designers, including Graeme North and Young and Richards, and finished the build in less than a year. Six Earthship experts from overseas joined friends, family and the couple's three children to help with the work. The children were aged 14, 12 and four at the time. Rowe and Anning stayed at the site every day to keep the project on track. They also prepared meals for the workers, who helped turn their plans into a home.Passive design and repurposed materialsThe house is designed to manage heat, airflow and water through its layout and building materials, rather than depending on standard heating and cooling systems. According to OneRoof, the four-bedroom home is built one room deep. Every room faces north towards the sun and opens onto a conservatory corridor filled with plants. Anning explained that the design helps keep the temperature steady and makes sure every room gets sunlight. "Because we live in New Zealand, it's not such a harsh climate," Anning said, as reported by OneRoof. "We opened it out [with] a free-flowing, indoor-outdoor flow. Every room faced north for the sun [and] every room gets the same amount of sun. There's no back corner."He also described how the house stays warm and cool throughout the year. "The house sits about 20 degrees [Celsius] all year round," Anning said, according to OneRoof. "As it's facing north, you've got 70-degree-angle glazing to accept more of that winter sun [and a] big thermal mass at the back in the tyres, which heat up." During summer, warm air can escape through a vent tube when the upper Velux windows are opened. This helps cool the house without relying on conventional air conditioning.Water and power systems are also built into the design. Greywater from the house flows into a planted area inside the atrium, where it is used to water the plants. Solar panels generate electricity for the household, with any extra power able to be sent back to the grid. The recycled glass bottles are used as decorative features and also help with insulation. Trade Me Property reported that the home has received five million views since appearing on television.Family life and moving northRowe said living in the house had been an important experience for the couple and their children. She described how the building responds to changes in temperature and humidity."It's insanely holistic," Rowe said, as reported by OneRoof. "It breathes and regulates the humidity and the temperature."She said the project had also taught the family a great deal about living with natural resources and making use of their surroundings. "Learning about harnessing solar energy, rainwater collection and the whole beauty of the surroundings," Rowe said, according to OneRoof. "It's been a vision that came to life and a really, really special place to call home."The family is now preparing to move to the Bay of Islands, where Anning has family roots. He works as a professional skipper and expedition guide and sees the move as the start of another stage in their lives. "It's just another chapter," Anning said, as reported by OneRoof. "It's awesome to mix it up a bit. It's quite a short time that we're here. We only live once, really. Bring it on."Agent reaction and search for new custodiansListing agent Heather Sturgeon had watched the Grand Designs NZ episode featuring the house. She also knew Rowe and Anning from meeting them at a nearby swimming hole before she became involved in the sale, OneRoof reported. Sturgeon said seeing the property in person helped her understand the amount of work that had gone into building it."It was nothing I've ever seen before," Sturgeon said, according to OneRoof. "I'd watched the episode. That gave a lot of context to how much work and man-hours went into building this property. But it was amazing to see it in person, and just the scale of it was exceptional."She particularly praised the plant-filled corridor, which receives natural light from skylights, and the glass bottles used throughout the house. Among them were blue Bombay Sapphire bottles, which caught her attention. Trade Me Property reported that the listing had a deadline sale date of 9 November 2026.Rowe said the family hopes the next owners will appreciate the work and ideas behind the property and continue to care for it. "We're just willing to see it begin a new chapter with owners that will love it as much," Rowe said, as reported by OneRoof. "It feels like it has profound magic in its walls. And I really believe that it's calling its new owners right now. We believe that we'll find people that appreciate the vision we had behind it and just want to continue."You use AI every day. articles.summary: MUMBAI: A 60-year-old woman was sexually assaulted and hit on her forehead inside a public washroom at Ghatkopar railway station late on Thursday.
articles.body: MUMBAI: A 60-year-old woman was sexually assaulted and hit on her forehead inside a public washroom at Ghatkopar railway station late on Thursday. The Government Railway Police (GRP) arrested a 25-year-old man for the offence on Friday.The incident highlights glaring security lapses at suburban railway stations.The woman lives in Khadavli and comes to Ghatkopar, where she works as a daily wager. On Thursday, she was accompanied by her 18-year-old daughter.After finishing her work, she and her daughter went to Ghatkopar railway station to take a train to Khadavli. While her daughter waited on platform no. 2, the woman went to a washroom at 11.12 pm.The washroom was unmanned. CCTV cameras captured a man in his twenties entering the washroom shortly afterwards.Police said the man locked the washroom door from inside and sexually assaulted the woman in the passage. Cameras captured him leaving the washroom at 11.19 pm and hurrying in the direction of Ghatkopar Metro.Police said he also assaulted the woman on her forehead.Around 11.22 pm, the woman stepped out of the washroom and informed her daughter. They approached the GRP desk on platform no. 4 for help.The station manager and the Railway Protection Force (RPF) were informed. A policewoman questioned her, following which she narrated what had happened. The police took her to Rajawadi Hospital in Ghatkopar for a further medical examination.CCTV footage of Ghatkopar railway station was checked, and images of the accused were found. He had been captured on camera while entering and exiting the washroom. Police also checked CCTV footage in the vicinity of the railway station and Metro.A case of rape was registered under provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.Several teams were formed to track down the culprit.Police found leads from CCTV footage and tracked him down to Asalpha in Ghatkopar. articles.title: A runway planned for a giant Everglades airport became a pilot-training facility, then an immigration detention center called Alligator Alcatraz in 2025; the facility was permanently shut down in June 2026
articles.summary: Explore the fascinating transformation of Florida's Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport from a potential supersonic jetport to a high-profile immigration detention center known as Alligator Alcatraz, and its abrupt closure amidst controversy.
articles.body: Over the last few decades, one Florida runway served numerous purposes, transitioning from an unbuilt supersonic airport to an aviation training center and ultimately into a detention center. According to the Miami-Dade Aviation Department, the Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport (TNT) was built to provide a precision-instrument landing and training facility in South Florida for commercial pilots, private training sessions, and military touch-and-go operations.Before its 2025 conversion, commercial jets and military aircraft used the strip regularly. The department also reported that the airport held an Annual Service Volume capacity of almost 175,500 operations, though landings for all aircraft requiring user fees or weighing more than 12,500 pounds operated on a Prior Permission Required (PPR) basis.Airside and landside facilities The airside facilities at the Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport offered proper support to both large and small aircraft, providing a safe space for precise landings. As per the Miami-Dade Aviation Department, the airfield had a single asphalt runway, Runway 09/27, measuring 10,499 feet long and 150 feet wide.In addition, the asphalt was in good condition with High-Intensity Runway Lights. It also featured a 75-foot-wide parallel taxiway equipped with Medium-Intensity Taxiway Lights. On the other hand, the landside facilities consisted of only a 2,000-square-foot administration building, with no T-hangars, conventional hangars, fuel tanks, or tie-downs at the site, reflecting its strict role as a touch-and-go training strip with no overnight aircraft parking or refueling services.History of Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport Construction began in 1968 on the Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport, which was initially envisioned as the Everglades Jetport. The original runway, which opened in 1970, was designed to replace Miami International Airport and serve South Florida. However, fierce environmental opposition led President Richard Nixon to halt further development in January 1970 through the Everglades Jetport Pact, limiting the facility to its single training strip.The 24,960-acre property contained almost 900 acres of developed and operational land, while the remaining area was managed by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (formerly known as the Florida Game and Freshwater Fish Commission). Following its initial build, the airport’s most significant upgrades included a $3.5 million runway resurfacing and lighting enhancement in 1992 and a $100,000 taxiway restoration in 1996, as reported by the Miami-Dade Aviation Department. In recent years, Miami-Dade County focused on new strategies to generate revenue from the property.From training strip to Alligator AlcatrazIn June 2025, Florida officials partnered with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to convert the Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport into a large-scale immigration detention center dubbed “Alligator Alcatraz,” as reported by Britannica. The project was proposed by Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier and expedited by Governor Ron DeSantis, who made use of emergency powers to take control of the site despite its ownership by Miami-Dade County.The facility was set up to hold up to 5,000 detainees awaiting deportation under an expanded federal enforcement initiative. It began operating deportation flights by July 25, 2025, as per an announcement made by DeSantis. At the same time, the project landed in legal trouble after being criticized by civil rights groups, environmental organizations, legal experts, politicians, Indigenous communities, as well as the general public, who raised questions about the facility’s location, purpose, and authorization process.As per CBS News Miami, Governor DeSantis announced the permanent shutdown of the facility on June 25, 2026, after federal officials shifted all the remaining detainees to other immigration centres earlier that month ahead of the approaching hurricane season.You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Centre has proposed increasing the number of Lok Sabha seats by 50% for every state and Union territory, along with a similar increase in
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Centre has proposed increasing the number of Lok Sabha seats by 50% for every state and Union territory, along with a similar increase in the strength of their legislative assemblies, to implement one-third reservation for women.This is the Centre's second attempt to push the legislation after its earlier proposal was defeated in the Lok Sabha in April this year.The earlier three Bills were introduced to facilitate the setting up of a Delimitation Commission to readjust the allocation of seats in the Lok Sabha and state and Union territory assemblies, besides redrawing constituency boundaries.The fresh Bill, set to be introduced in the Lok Sabha on Monday, makes substantial changes to the original legislation, particularly in the constitution of the Delimitation Commission, the use of Census figures, the allocation of seats reserved for women and the expansion of legislative representation."The objective of the present Bill is to give immediate effect to one-third reservation for women, including women belonging to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, in the House of the People and the Legislative Assemblies of the states and the Union territories, through a delimitation exercise," the Bill's Statement of Objects and Reasons says.What is in the new BillThe Constitution (132nd Amendment) Bill, 2026, proposes to increase the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha to 850, with up to 815 members from states and 35 from Union territories.It also proposes to raise the maximum strength of a state legislative assembly from 500 to 650.It further proposes a 50% increase in the number of seats in the Lok Sabha and state and Union territory assemblies over their existing strength before the delimitation exercise.The Bill provides that the women's quota will remain in force for 15 years from the commencement of the 2023 amendment, with Parliament empowered to extend it through legislation.Parliament will also decide the authority and manner in which seats reserved for women will be rotated.Another key change is that the Centre will have to constitute the Delimitation Commission as soon as possible after the proposed legislation comes into force. The original Bill provided for setting up the commission "from time to time".The fresh Bill seeks to enable the rollout of the women's quota after the first delimitation exercise under the proposed amendment. The exercise will use the latest Census figures published by the time the law comes into force. This means the 2011 Census data will be used if no newer figures are published by then. The Delimitation Commission will use these figures to readjust seat allocations and redraw territorial constituencies.”Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: WHO warns measles progress has stalled as misinformation and low vaccination rates threaten elimination
articles.summary: The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued a stark warning about the stagnation of measles elimination efforts globally, citing misinformation and low vaccination rates as major hurdles. Discover the alarming trends and their implications for public health.
articles.body: The World Health Organization (WHO) has warned that global efforts to eliminate measles have lost momentum, with vaccination coverage remaining below the levels needed to prevent transmission and misinformation contributing to vaccine hesitancy, AFP reported.The warning comes a week after the United States lost its measles elimination status, following a rise in cases linked to declining vaccination rates. The WHO said the Covid-19 pandemic had also disrupted immunisation programmes worldwide, leaving several countries struggling to restore coverage to pre-pandemic levels and reach children who missed vaccinations during the crisis.WHO vaccines chief Kate O'Brien described the situation in the US as a reminder of how quickly preventable diseases can return when immunisation rates fall."Are we ringing the alarm bell about the number of children who are unvaccinated or under vaccinated? Absolutely. Measles is the most infectious virus known to humans," O'Brien said at a press conference at the agency's headquarters in Geneva."It is back -- and the world is learning just how sick and just how dead measles can make you."Global vaccination coverage remains below targetIn its assessment, the WHO said progress against measles had stalled in recent years. The estimated share of children receiving their first vaccine dose remained at 84% in 2025, unchanged from the previous year and below the 86% recorded in 2019, before the pandemic.Coverage for the second dose stood at 77% in 2025, matching an all-time high. The agency attributed the figure partly to more countries including the second dose in their routine immunisation programmes.Gabon and the Central African Republic are the only two WHO member states that have yet to introduce a second measles vaccine dose into their routine schedules.However, the agency said at least 95% coverage with both doses is necessary to interrupt transmission and protect communities.An estimated 20.8 million children did not receive any measles vaccine in 2025, while another 8.3 million received only one dose. Although the proportion of unvaccinated children remained stable, their overall number increased as the global number of newborns rose.Measles typically affects children and can cause fever, respiratory symptoms and skin rashes. In severe cases, it can lead to pneumonia and inflammation of the brain, potentially resulting in permanent complications or death. Children are generally offered two doses of the vaccine by the time they are 18 months old.WHO flags misinformation and political polarisationThe WHO also identified misinformation and disinformation as major obstacles to improving vaccine uptake, saying they were contributing to confusion among parents about immunisation.O'Brien said vaccine discussions had become increasingly tied to political and ideological divisions in several countries."Misinformation and disinformation" were a significant contributor to parents being "confused about what they should be doing", she said.The US has reported more than 5,400 measles cases this year, marking its worst outbreak in more than three decades, according to AFP. Medical experts have criticised Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr, a prominent vaccine sceptic, over his repeated questioning of vaccine safety, arguing that such statements have fuelled public distrust.O'Brien also cautioned against the practice of deliberately exposing children to measles, sometimes described as attending 'measles parties', in an attempt to develop immunity."Exposing children to measles is a terrible idea," she said, rejecting the notion that contracting the infection was a normal part of growing up."I really want to dispel this idea that measles is some rite of passage of childhood. It's not. It's a serious illness for which we have a safe and effective vaccine."Measles vaccination has saved more than 60 million livesDespite the setbacks, the WHO highlighted the impact of vaccination programmes over the past two decades. Measles immunisation since 2000 is estimated to have prevented more than 60 million deaths, making it the most life-saving childhood vaccination effort over the past 50 years, according to O'Brien.WHO modelling estimates that there were around 9.8 million measles cases and 72,000 deaths worldwide in 2025. The death toll was the lowest on record, while annual cases had fallen from an estimated 37.8 million in 2000, as cited by AFP.However, outbreaks remained widespread. Fifty-nine countries experienced large or disruptive measles outbreaks last year, including 28 in the African region and 13 in Europe. Eleven of those countries had either previously received verification of measles elimination or were currently verified as having eliminated the disease.The WHO said 92 countries had been verified as having achieved or maintained measles elimination.You use AI every day. articles.title: Canada's Supreme Court largely upholds Quebec's 2019 law banning certain public workers from wearing religious symbols at work, including Sikh turbans, Muslim hijabs and Christian crosses
articles.summary: Canada's Supreme Court has upheld most of Quebec's controversial Bill 21, which prevents certain public sector employees from wearing religious symbols
articles.body: Canada's Supreme Court has upheld most of Quebec's controversial Bill 21, which prevents certain public sector employees from wearing religious symbols while performing their jobs. The ruling, delivered on November 27, 2026, confirms that the province can enforce the restrictions despite challenges based on religious freedom, equality and minority rights. The decision means that public school teachers, police officers, government lawyers and other officials covered by the legislation must continue to follow the restrictions. Religious items affected include Sikh turbans, Muslim hijabs, Jewish kippahs and visible Christian crosses.However, the court identified a constitutional problem with one part of the law. It ruled that the requirement for members of Quebec's National Assembly to uncover their faces violates their democratic rights when it prevents elected representatives from taking part in legislative proceedings. In its judgment in English Montreal School Board v. Quebec (Attorney General), 2026 SCC 41, the Supreme Court also rejected the argument that Bill 21 violates the education rights of Quebec's English-speaking minority. This means English-language school boards will not receive the exemption sought in the case. The ruling follows years of legal challenges and confirms the Quebec government's ability to use Canada's constitutional notwithstanding clause to protect the legislation from certain Charter challenges. The Supreme Court's official summary states that the appeals were dismissed, along with the Quebec government's cross-appeal.The origins and implementation of Bill 21The Quebec government, led by Premier François Legault of the Coalition Avenir Québec party at the time, introduced and passed Bill 21 in June 2019. The legislation was presented as a way to protect state secularism, known in French as laïcité, and ensure that government representatives maintain religious neutrality while carrying out their duties. The law prohibits certain public employees in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols while working. Those covered include public school teachers, police officers, judges, prosecutors and prison guards.The Quebec government argued that people exercising state authority should not display religious beliefs while performing their official duties. Supporters said the legislation would help maintain a clear separation between religion and the state. The measure faced strong opposition from religious minority communities and civil liberties organisations. Critics argued that it forced people to choose between their religious beliefs and their careers, particularly those who wear visible religious clothing as part of their faith.The government also invoked the notwithstanding clause when passing the legislation. Section 33 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms allows federal or provincial legislatures to keep certain laws in force despite some Charter protections, including fundamental freedoms and equality rights. Such an override lasts for up to five years and can be renewed. Quebec also invoked the relevant override provision in its own Charter of human rights and freedoms. This made it more difficult for opponents to have Bill 21 overturned through challenges based on the rights covered by those clauses. The Supreme Court has now confirmed that Quebec used these powers validly.Immediate opposition and legal challengesBill 21 prompted legal challenges from civil liberties groups, teachers' organisations and members of religious communities soon after it became law. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association (CCLA) and the National Council of Canadian Muslims (NCCM) were among the organisations involved in challenging the legislation. Opponents argued that the ban violated freedom of conscience and religion, as well as equality rights protected by the Canadian Charter. They also said its effects were particularly serious for religious minorities and women who wear religious clothing. Critics maintained that the restrictions created difficult choices for public employees. Teachers who wear hijabs, turbans or other religious symbols could be forced to leave their jobs, move elsewhere or stop following religious practices to continue working in the public education system. The debate also raised concerns about hostility towards visible religious minorities in Quebec.The case moved through the province's courts before reaching Canada's highest court. On February 29, 2024, the Quebec Court of Appeal upheld most of the earlier ruling and rejected the argument that Bill 21 violated the minority-language education rights of English-speaking communities. The Court of Appeal concluded that the legislation dealt with hiring practices rather than the language of instruction or the content of educational programmes. Several parties then appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada, which heard the case over four days, from March 23 to March 26, 2026. The hearing involved 51 interveners, including six provincial and territorial attorneys general.The Supreme Court's nuanced judgmentThe Supreme Court's decision addressed several constitutional questions, including the use of the notwithstanding clause, equality rights, minority-language education rights and the democratic rights of elected representatives. One of the main issues was whether Quebec had legally used the notwithstanding clause to protect Bill 21 from challenges based on certain Charter rights. The court confirmed that the provincial government had used the clause validly. It also ruled that courts retain the power to examine whether legislation conflicts with Charter rights, even when a government has invoked the override clause. A court can make a declaration that a law is inconsistent with those rights, although the Supreme Court did not make such a declaration in this case. The judges also considered Section 28 of the Canadian Charter, which states that the rights and freedoms guaranteed by the Charter apply equally to men and women.The court ruled that Section 28 does not create a separate right that can independently be used to challenge legislation. As a result, Bill 21 could not be struck down on that basis. Another important issue concerned Section 23, which protects the education rights of English-speaking and French-speaking minorities in Canada. The English Montreal School Board argued that Bill 21 interfered with its ability to recruit, retain, transfer and promote teachers who wear religious symbols. It said the restrictions affected the board's constitutional right to manage its schools and protect the interests of Quebec's English-speaking community.The Supreme Court acknowledged that the legislation could limit the board's ability to hire and retain certain employees. However, the majority found that there was not enough evidence to establish that these restrictions undermined the specific linguistic and cultural interests protected by Section 23. The court therefore rejected the request for an exemption. English-language public schools in Quebec must continue to follow the religious symbols ban. The judges did identify a separate problem involving Section 8 of Bill 21. This provision requires members of Quebec's National Assembly to keep their faces uncovered while carrying out their legislative duties. The court found that this requirement infringes Section 3 of the Canadian Charter, which protects citizens' democratic rights, including the right to seek election and participate in legislative proceedings. It ruled that elected representatives whose religious beliefs require them to wear face coverings cannot be prevented from taking part in the legislature because of that requirement.Reactions and future implicationsThe Supreme Court's ruling has drawn attention from supporters and opponents of Bill 21 across Canada. Quebec's supporters have welcomed the decision as confirmation that the province has the authority to protect its model of state secularism. The ruling also reinforces the government's ability to use the notwithstanding clause when passing legislation that it believes reflects the province's priorities. The English Montreal School Board expressed disappointment after losing its appeal. In a statement published on November 27, 2026, the board highlighted that the decision was reached by a narrow 4-3 majority on the constitutionality of Bill 21. The board also pointed out that three judges would have allowed its appeal on the basis that the law improperly infringed Section 28 of the Charter. Two judges would have found that the legislation violated Section 23, while another judge did not decide that issue after finding a breach of Section 28.Civil liberties organisations and religious minority advocates have continued to raise concerns about the effects of the legislation. Their objections centre on the restrictions placed on people who wish to work in public positions without giving up visible expressions of their religious beliefs. The ruling also has wider implications for Canadian constitutional law, particularly the use of the notwithstanding clause. By confirming that governments can invoke the provision without facing additional limits beyond those written into the clause, the Supreme Court has reinforced the power of provincial legislatures to protect certain laws from Charter challenges. At the same time, the decision confirms that courts can still examine whether legislation conflicts with constitutional rights, even when an override has been used. The November 27 judgment settles the main constitutional challenge to Quebec's Bill 21, leaving the religious symbols restrictions in place for covered public employees. The specific requirement that elected members of the National Assembly uncover their faces, however, has been found to violate their democratic rights.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
